newsitem.title: CHINA: Cloning seen helping save China's panda.
newsitem.headline: Cloning seen helping save China's panda.

text.p: Two of China's top geneticists said on Monday they saw newly-developed cloning techniques as being hugely useful for animal research, and could provide a means of helping to save the endangered Giant Panda.
But they said the use of cloning with humans had raised many sensitive issues which needed to be handled at a national level.

Professor Li Changben, at Fudan University's Institute of Genetics, said in an interview that cloning of a living organism was very much like nuclear technology -- it had the power to be used for both incalculable good and evil.
"There are always two sides to scientific advances like this," Li said. "For instance, we can use this technique to prevent the extinction of the panda and other endangered species."

It is estimated that there are now only about 1,000 Giant Pandas left in the wild, in the bamboo forests of southwestern China. China has panda breeding programmes in a number of zoos, but the success rate has proved very low.
Eight panda cubs were born in captivity last year of which only three survived.

Professor Zhao Shouyuan, vice-chairman of the China Genetics Society, said it would be three or four years before China was able to do what British scientists announced they had done recently with the cloning in Scotland of Dolly the sheep.
"We should speed up work in this area, but our view is that you shouldn't allow everyone who wants to, to do it," Zhao said. "It should be restricted to chosen research centres."
He said China would focus its cloning research on projects which had the potential to make money, such as engineering of pigs, cows and sheep to raise productivity.
But he said there was also much that cloning could contribute to research in general.
"It has huge value for raising animals for use in experiments, for instance. If the animals are exactly the same physiologically, it makes experiments much easier to control," he said.

"It will also help to save endangered species like the panda. But it would be best to not create exact copies, but to use genetic engineering to come up with versions that are better than the original," he said.
Zhao said the use of cloning on humans was an issue that needed to be considered at a national level.
"The country needs to consider all kinds of opinions, as a result of which I am sure a wise decision will emerge," he said.

"The technique should be developed, but not for use on humans," said Professor Li. "But then there will be examples like childless couples who want to use this. How to judge where the line is? There needs to be a law."
Zhao said the cloning technique was not something to be feared because no two organisms could ever be the same because of differing environmental factors.

"Cloning is like nuclear energy. The first reaction of people to nuclear power was terror, but it later became clear there were useful aspects to the technology which could be used for peaceful purposes," Zhao said.
